summary.text: Solubility is the ability of a substance, the solute, to form a solution with another substance, the solvent.
It is usually measured as the concentration of the solute in a saturated solution, one in which no more solute can be dissolved.
It depends mainly on the make-up of the solute and solvent, along with temperature and pressure.

facts.label: Saturated solution
facts.value: No more solute can be dissolved in it

facts.label: Miscible
facts.value: Two substances that mix in all proportions

facts.label: Handbook unit
facts.value: Often g/(100 mL), grams of solute per 100 millilitres of solvent

facts.label: One cut-off for insoluble
facts.value: Under 0.1 g per 100 mL of solvent

items.prompt: A solution is holding more dissolved solute than it normally could. A speck appears for crystals to start forming on. What happens?

options.label: Nothing, because the extra solute stays dissolved for good
The solvent boils away
The excess solute comes out of solution rapidly
The solute turns into a gas

items.explain: Such a supersaturated solution is metastable and rapidly excludes the excess solute if a suitable nucleation site appears.

items.prompt: Stirring a solid into water makes it dissolve faster. Does the stirring change the most that can dissolve?

options.label: Yes, stirring raises the solubility by the same factor
No, stirring changes how fast it dissolves, which is a different thing from solubility
Yes, stirring is the main thing solubility depends on
No, because a solid can never dissolve faster

items.explain: Solubility is not the same as the rate of solution, which depends on variables such as the manner and intensity of mixing.

items.prompt: A chemist pours hydrochloric acid on calcium hydroxide and it vanishes. Informally one might say it dissolved. Does solubility apply?

options.label: No, because an irreversible chemical reaction takes place between them
Yes, since anything that vanishes in a liquid has dissolved
Yes, but only if the acid is cooled first
No, because acids can never act as a solvent

items.explain: The concept of solubility does not apply when there is an irreversible chemical reaction between the two substances.

items.prompt: A solution is saturated and nothing seems to change. What is happening among the particles?

options.label: Dissolving has stopped, but re-joining carries on
Re-joining has stopped, but dissolving carries on
Neither process can happen once it is saturated
Dissolving and re-joining are going on at equal rates

items.explain: Solubility occurs under dynamic equilibrium, with a stable state when the rates of dissolution and re-joining are equal.

items.prompt: A chemist wants to dissolve a solid in a gas. What has to happen first?

options.label: The solid has to pass into the gaseous state
The gas has to be cooled down until it condenses
The solid has to be ground into a fine powder
The gas has to be pressurised until it behaves like a liquid

items.explain: A solid or liquid can be dissolved in a gas only by passing into the gaseous state first.

items.prompt: Ethanol mixes with water at any ratio, with no limit. What word applies to this?

options.label: Saturated
Miscible
Supersaturated
Insoluble

items.explain: Substances with no solubility limit are miscible in all proportions, such as ethanol in water.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Solubility is the ability of one substance, the solute, to form a solution with another, the solvent. Its opposite, insolubility, is the inability to form such a solution. A solute may be solid, liquid or gaseous, while the solvent is usually a solid or a liquid.

paragraphs.heading: Saturation and balance
paragraphs.text: Solubility is usually measured as the concentration of solute in a saturated solution, one that cannot dissolve any more. At that point the two substances are at the solubility equilibrium. This balance is dynamic. Dissolving and its reverse, such as a solid coming back out as a precipitate, go on at the same time, and a stable state is reached when their rates are equal.

paragraphs.heading: Mixing without limit
paragraphs.text: Some pairs have no limit at all and are called miscible, meaning they mix in all proportions. Gases are always miscible with each other, except in very extreme situations. Solubility ranges from ethanol in water, which mixes without limit, to titanium dioxide, which is essentially insoluble in water.

paragraphs.heading: What controls it
paragraphs.text: Solubility depends mainly on what the solute and solvent are made of, including their pH and any other dissolved substances, and on temperature and pressure. These effects can often be explained by how the particles of the two substances interact, and by thermodynamic ideas such as enthalpy and entropy. Solubility also differs from the rate of solution, meaning how fast a solid dissolves in a liquid. That rate depends on other things, such as the physical form of the substances and how hard they are mixed.

paragraphs.heading: Going past the limit
paragraphs.text: Under certain conditions a solution can hold more solute than its usual limit. The result is called a supersaturated solution. It will quickly push out the extra solute once a suitable nucleation site appears.

paragraphs.heading: How it is written
paragraphs.text: Chemical handbooks often give solubility as grams of solute per 100 mL of solvent, or as grams per 100 g of solvent. It can also be given in moles, for example as moles of solute per litre of solution, the molarity. Converting between these units can be tricky, because it may call for the density of the solution, a figure that often goes unmeasured.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Solubility matters well beyond chemistry, in fields such as geology, biology, medicine and agriculture, and even in cooking, cleaning and brewing. Most useful chemical reactions only take place after the ingredients have been dissolved in a suitable solvent. Water is by far the most common choice.
